facts.statement: Shuvosaurus is a beaked, bipedal pseudosuchian from the Late Triassic of western Texas.
facts.quote: Shuvosaurus (meaning "Shuvo [Chatterjee]'s lizard") is a genus of beaked, bipedal poposauroid pseudosuchian from the Late Triassic (early to middle Norian) of western Texas.

facts.statement: Although Shuvosaurus looks like a theropod dinosaur, it is more closely related to modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: Despite superficially resembling a theropod dinosaur, especially the ostrich-like ornithomimids, it is instead more closely related to living crocodilians than to dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Shuvosaurus fossils were collected in 1984 and formally described in 1993 by Sankar Chatterjee.
facts.quote: Fossils of Shuvosaurus were first discovered and collected in 1984, but were not described until 1993 by palaeontologist Sankar Chatterjee.

facts.statement: The name Shuvosaurus honors Sankar Chatterjee's son, Shuvo, combining his name with the Greek word for lizard.
facts.quote: Chatterjee recognized its distinctiveness in the late 1980s during preparation by his younger son Shuvo Chatterjee, for whom he named it after (combining "Shuvo" with the Ancient Greek σαῦρος (sauros), meaning "lizard").

facts.statement: Shuvosaurus lived during the early to middle Norian stage of the Late Triassic, approximately 224 to 215 million years ago.
facts.quote: it has been correlated to the Adamanian teilzone, a local biostratigraphic unit in the southwestern United States—that has elsewhere been dated to the early to middle Norian stage of the Late Triassic, between 224–215 million years old

facts.statement: The original description of Shuvosaurus included three skulls, a partial lower jaw, and a partial atlas vertebra.
facts.quote: These original fossils consisted of the partially disarticulated remains of three skulls and a partial lower jaw (the holotype TTU (Texas Tech University)-P9280 and paratypes TTU-P9281 and TTU-P9282), as well as a partial atlas and fragmentary vertebra, scapula and an informally referred tibia.

facts.statement: Most postcranial bones originally assigned to Shuvosaurus were later reidentified as belonging to other animals.
facts.quote: Of these postcranial bones only the atlas belongs to Shuvosaurus, the others have since been reidentified as belonging to an azendohsaurid, an ornithodiran and a neotheropod dinosaur, respectively.

facts.statement: Shuvosaurus fossils were found in a bonebed containing at least nine associated skeletons and a minimum of 14 individuals based on femur counts.
facts.quote: The fossils of Shuvosaurus were preserved in a bonebed containing the remains of at least nine partially articulated and associated skeletons alongside the skeleton of a Postosuchus, with a minimum total of 14 individuals indicated by the number of right partial femurs collected.

facts.statement: Sankar Chatterjee originally interpreted Shuvosaurus as a Triassic ornithomimosaur dinosaur based on its toothless jaws and large eye sockets.
facts.quote: Upon its description, Chatterjee tentatively interpreted Shuvosaurus as a Triassic member of Ornithomimosauria, a group of theropod dinosaurs otherwise known only from the Cretaceous, due to similar construction of the skull, including toothless jaws and large eye sockets.

facts.statement: The species name *inexpectatus* reflects the surprise of finding a toothless, ostrich-mimic-like skull in Late Triassic rocks.
facts.quote: This is reflected in the species name, inexpectatus, for the unexpected nature of finding a toothless, ornithomimid-like skull in Late Triassic deposits.

facts.statement: Chatterjee's hypothesis that Shuvosaurus was a dinosaur was met with skepticism by researchers like Halszka Osmólska.
facts.quote: As with the contemporary purported avian Protoavis and Postosuchus, Chatterjee's proposed affinities of a Late Triassic Post Quarry taxon to Cretaceous coelurosaurs invoked a long ghost lineage and was consequently greeted with skepticism by other researchers (such as Halszka Osmólska in 1997).

facts.statement: In 1995, Long and Murry described the skull material as a new taxon named *Chatterjeea elegans*.
facts.quote: However, in a 1995 monograph on Late Triassic tetrapods from the American Southwest, Robert Long and Philip Murry regarded this material as so "radically different" from Postosuchus that they identified it as a new taxon of gracile "rauisuchian" allied to poposaurids (i.e. Poposaurus) which they named Chatterjeea elegans—named after Sankar Chatterjee and from Latin elegans for "very fine" or "beautiful".

facts.statement: Oliver Rauhut argued that *Shuvosaurus* was a distinct theropod dinosaur that evolved traits similar to ornithomimosaurs.
facts.quote: Following Long and Murry (1995), opinions were divided on the identity of Shuvosaurus and its proposed synonymy with Chatterjeea. Notable among them, Oliver Rauhut (1997, 2000, 2003) argued that Shuvosaurus was indeed a theropod and distinct from Chatterjeea, but that it was instead a specialised basal taxon convergent with ornithomimosaurs.

facts.statement: In 2006, Nesbitt and Norell named *Effigia* based on fossils combining a *Shuvosaurus*-like skull with *Chatterjeea*-like body parts.
facts.quote: In the early 2000s, Sterling Nesbitt and Mark Norell prepared previously unopened plaster-jackets of an unknown archosaur collected from the Whitaker Quarry at Ghost Ranch which combined a Shuvosaurus-like skull with Chatterjeea-like postcrania that they named Effigia in 2006.

facts.statement: The discovery of *Effigia* proved that *Shuvosaurus* is a pseudosuchian related to crocodilians and that *Shuvosaurus* and *Chatterjeea* are synonymous.
facts.quote: This discovery showed that Shuvosaurus is more closely related to crocodilians and other pseudosuchians than dinosaurs, and that similarities between it and ornithomimids are indeed the result of convergent evolution, while simultaneously demonstrating that the bodies of Chatterjeea almost certainly belong to Shuvosaurus and therefore that the two are synonymous.

facts.statement: In 2007, Spencer Lucas and colleagues proposed merging *Effigia* into *Shuvosaurus* as the species *S. okeeffeae*.
facts.quote: Shuvosaurus and Effigia are so anatomically similar that in 2007 Spencer Lucas and colleagues proposed that the two genera were synonymous, tentatively subsuming Effigia into Shuvosaurus as the species Shuvosaurus okeeffeae.

facts.statement: *Shuvosaurus* was thoroughly re-examined and redescribed in late 2023 and early 2024.
facts.quote: Shuvosaurus itself would not be thoroughly re-examined for many years until late 2023 and early 2024, when two separate redescriptions were published independently.

facts.statement: Lehane redescribed the skull in 2023, followed by a complete skeletal osteology by Nesbitt and Chatterjee in 2024.
facts.quote: First, the skull was redescribed by Lehane (2023), based upon the work of his previously unpublished 2005 master's thesis. This study was followed shortly after by a complete skeletal osteology from Nesbitt and Chatterjee (2024).

facts.statement: In 2024, Nesbitt and Chatterjee restricted *Shuvosaurus* to the material from the Post Quarry bonebed.
facts.quote: Following their osteological description, Nesbitt and Chatterjee revised the taxonomic diagnosis of Shuvosaurus in 2024 and in doing so restricted Shuvosaurus to the type and associated material of the Post Quarry bonebed alone, as isolated bones cannot be reliably differentiated between the two genera.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses consistently place Shuvosaurus as a close relative of Effigia and the South American Sillosuchus.
facts.quote: Phylogenetic analyses since then consistently find Shuvosaurus as a close relative of Effigia and the South American Sillosuchus

facts.statement: Until 2026, Shuvosaurus and Effigia were consistently recovered as sister taxa within the family Shuvosauridae.
facts.quote: Up until 2026, Shuvosaurus and Effigia were consistently found to be sister taxa within Shuvosauridae

facts.statement: The relationships between North American shuvosaurids, including Shuvosaurus, remain unresolved in recent analyses.
facts.quote: However, the relationships between the North American shuvosaurids (a subclade Smith and Sidor labelled "Node A") are unresolved

facts.statement: Chatterjee argued that convergent evolution was unlikely, believing the skull features were distinctly ornithomimosaurian.
facts.quote: However, he himself considered convergent evolution unlikely in this case based on his interpretation of the morphological evidence that otherwise appeared distinctly ornithomimosaurian.

facts.statement: Later researchers argued that Chatterjee had not definitively proven the skull belonged to a dinosaur.
facts.quote: Hunt et al. (1998) and Heckert & Lucas (1998) went even further and argued that although Chatterjee (1993) compared specific features of Shuvosaurus strongly to ornithomimosaurs, he had not demonstrated that the skull was definitively even that of a dinosaur in the first place.

facts.statement: In a 2003 analysis, Rauhut recovered Shuvosaurus as a coelophysoid theropod.
facts.quote: Rauhut later included Shuvosaurus in a phylogenetic analysis of theropods in 2003, in which it was recovered as a coelophysoid.

facts.statement: James Lehane revised his classification of Shuvosaurus in 2023 after the discovery of Effigia.
facts.quote: Lehane later revised this classification when formally publishing his description of the skull in 2023, subsequent to the discovery of Effigia.

facts.statement: The group containing Shuvosaurus and Poposaurus was later defined as the clade Poposauroidea.
facts.quote: This grouping of Poposaurus-like taxa was later defined as the clade Poposauroidea.

facts.statement: Shuvosaurus lived from the Norian to the Rhaetian stages, between 227.3 and 201.4 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Norian to Rhaetian (227.3 to 201.4 million years ago)
